excerpt: An expired license does not bar an injury claim in Georgia or South Carolina. How courts separate a paperwork lapse from crash causation.
keyTakeaways: An expired driver's license does not bar personal injury claims in Georgia or South Carolina. Courts distinguish between administrative violations and accident causation — an expired license does not cause collisions. Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) and South Carolina use modified comparative fault, reducing damages by fault percentage. Insurance companies may try to exploit an expired license, but Georgia's Court of Appeals held in 2025 that lack of a valid license 'does not, by itself, support a negligence claim' without a causal link to the crash, and South Carolina requires the same causal link. Georgia statute of limitations is 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33); South Carolina is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

faqs.question: Can I file an accident claim if my license was expired?
faqs.answer: Yes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, an expired license does not prevent you from filing a personal injury claim. Your right to compensation depends on who caused the accident, not whether your license was current. An expired license is an administrative issue that does not cause accidents.

faqs.question: Will the insurance company deny my claim because of an expired license?
faqs.answer: Insurance companies may try to deny your claim or reduce your settlement based on an expired license, but this is generally not legally supported. An expired license does not establish causation for the accident. Having an attorney handle insurance communications prevents them from exploiting this issue.

faqs.question: Is an expired license the same as a suspended license for injury claims?
faqs.answer: No. An expired license is a paperwork lapse. A suspended or revoked license is more serious — the state took the privilege away, sometimes for unsafe driving such as DUI and sometimes for unrelated reasons like an unpaid fine or a missed court date — and it can matter in a claim against an owner who lent the car (negligent entrustment). But in Georgia and South Carolina, even a suspended license does not by itself prove the driver caused the crash; there must be a causal connection (Thames v. Pinson, Ga. Ct. App. 2025, quoting Keenan v. Hill; Fairchild v. SCDOT, S.C. 2012, quoting Cartee v. Lesley).

faqs.question: Can an expired license be used against me in court?
faqs.answer: While driving with an expired license violates Georgia law (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-20) and South Carolina law (S.C. Code § 56-1-20), courts require that the violation be the proximate cause of the accident for it to affect fault. Since an expired license does not cause accidents, it typically fails the causation test.

faqs.question: What are the penalties for driving with an expired license?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, driving on an expired license is a misdemeanor punished under O.C.G.A. § 40-5-121(a): for a first conviction within five years, 2 days to 12 months in jail (which a judge may suspend or probate), and the court may add a fine of $500 to $1,000 — but if the license had been expired fewer than 31 days and you produce in court a license that would have been valid at the time, you are not guilty (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-20(a)(1)). In South Carolina, an expired license is not a valid license under S.C. Code § 56-1-20, and driving on one is a misdemeanor under S.C. Code § 56-1-440(A): a first offense carries a fine of $50 to $100 or 30 days in jail, a second offense $500 or 45 days or both, and a third or later offense 45 days to six months. The criminal case is separate from your civil injury claim.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for filing an accident claim?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, you have 2 years from the date of the accident (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, you have 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Do not let concerns about your expired license delay filing — the deadline applies regardless of your license status.
